explanation:
## The order, with the tool for each

| # | Stage | Tool | Stop after it with |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Preprocess | `cpp` | `gcc -E` |
| 2 | Lex | the compiler front end | — |
| 3 | Parse to an AST | the compiler front end | `-fdump-tree-original` |
| 4 | Instruction selection, register allocation | the compiler back end | `gcc -S` |
| 5 | Assemble | `as` | `gcc -c` |
| 6 | Link | `ld` | (produces the executable) |
| 7 | Dynamic load | `ld.so` | happens at **run** time |

The two that trip people up are at the ends.

**Assembling comes before linking.** Each source file is compiled and assembled on its own into a `.o`, and only then are the objects linked together. That is why a typo in one file is a *compile* error naming that file, while a missing function is a *link* error naming no file in particular — by then the compiler has forgotten which translation unit anything came from. It is also why you can rebuild one changed file and relink, which is the entire basis of `make`.

**Dynamic loading is not a build step.** It happens every time the program starts. That is why a missing shared library is not caught by a successful build and shows up as `error while loading shared libraries` when someone runs it on a different machine.

## Watching it happen

Every stage is inspectable, and doing this once is worth more than reading about it:

```bash
gcc -E hello.c -o hello.i     # preprocessed: one file, thousands of lines
gcc -S hello.c -o hello.s     # assembly text you can read
gcc -c hello.c -o hello.o     # an object file, not yet runnable
gcc hello.o -o hello          # linked
./hello
```

Two things are worth noticing when you do:

`hello.i` is enormous. A ten-line program that includes `<stdio.h>` preprocesses to a thousand-plus lines, because `#include` is literal textual inclusion. This is the whole reason C++ builds are slow and the reason modules exist.

`hello.s` is short and readable. Looking at your own code's assembly at `-O0` and then at `-O2` is the single most educational thing you can do with a compiler, and it is one command away.

## Where the errors come from

Knowing the stage tells you which tool is complaining, which is most of diagnosing a build:

- **Preprocessor**: `No such file or directory` for a header. An include-path problem — `-I`.
- **Parser**: `expected ';' before ...`. Grammar, in your file, at that line.
- **Semantic analysis**: `incompatible types`. Grammatical but meaningless.
- **Linker**: `undefined reference to 'foo'`. Everything compiled; nothing *defines* `foo`. You need the library — `-lfoo` — or you declared it and never wrote it.
- **Loader**: `error while loading shared libraries`. Built fine, cannot run here.

`undefined reference` is the one people misread most. It is never a syntax problem and never fixed by including another header: a header declares, and the linker needs a *definition*.

## The two stages this list simplifies

Real compilers put an optimiser between the AST and instruction selection, working on an intermediate representation — LLVM IR, or GCC's GIMPLE — and that is where nearly all the interesting work happens. And modern toolchains can defer code generation to link time entirely (`-flto`), which smears the boundary between stages 4 and 6 so that the optimiser can inline across translation units. The sequence above is still the right mental model; it is just that two of the boxes are bigger than they look.
